appraisal_events.evidence: To keep from wearying of Odette's now too-fixed manner, Swann deliberately sends her letters full of feigned disappointment and simulated anger, calculating that her fear of losing him will draw out words she has never said before; this ploy in fact produced the tenderest letters she had yet written him.
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann's manipulative provocation is presented as an effective tactic that keeps drawing fresh tenderness out of Odette, giving him working command over the emotional register of the relationship.

appraisal_events.evidence: Having dawdled with the young working girl, Swann arrives so late that Odette, thinking he would not come, has already left; seeing she is gone, he feels a genuine pang at heart and trembles at being deprived of a pleasure whose scale he measures for the first time, having always before been certain of finding it.
appraisal_events.explanation: The scene marks a reversal from Swann's usual confidence: for the first time he suffers real, unguarded dependency and loss rather than exercising control.

appraisal_events.evidence: M. Verdurin says to his wife, 'Did you see the face he made when he realized she wasn't there? I think we can say he's hooked!'
appraisal_events.explanation: M. Verdurin turns Swann's visible distress into a private joke, reducing his romantic vulnerability to an object of amusement observed by an onlooker.

status_effects.explanation: His deliberate provocation succeeds in drawing out Odette's most tender letters yet, giving him working command over the emotional register of the relationship at this point.

Swann suffers a genuine, unfamiliar pang of loss and vulnerability on finding Odette gone, revealing for the first time a real dependency rather than confident control over the pleasure of seeing her.
M. Verdurin's teasing remark that Swann is 'hooked' turns his visible infatuation into a source of private amusement rather than dignity.
